newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman convincingly ahead in election count.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman convincingly ahead in election count.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman appeared certain of a convincing re-election victory on Monday and promised to attack low living standards hit by war and recession.

With around 80 percent of the votes counted, election officials said it was unlikely Tudjman would be forced into a second round run-off against his nearest challenger, former communist Zdravko Tomac.
Tudjman needed 50 percent to win outright in the first round and had taken 59.8 percent of the votes counted.
Partial figures showed Tomac, now a Social Democratic, was in second place with 21.96 percent and Vlado Gotovac of the Croatian Social Liberal Party was third with 18.23 percent.
"It is very unlikely that there will be a second round," the deputy head of the state electoral commission, Jakov Miletic, told Reuters.
"Given the big difference between the candidates, it is unlikely the result will change much," he said.
Election officials said the turnout on Sunday was around 60 percent of the electorate.

Celebrating at a banquet as the first results came in, Tudjman told reporters: "I promise the continuity of the policy with which we established freedom and independence in Croatia, a stable economy and currency...
"We are leaving behind the state of war, now we shall dedicate ourselves with all our forces to raising the standards of living for the entire population."
Tudjman presided over a post-communist economic reform programme launched in 1993 which slashed inflation and stabilised the currency, boosting foreign investor interest and domestic growth.
But the majority of Croats are struggling to make ends meet after a war which destroyed infrastructure and closed factories.
The strong exchange rate hurts exports and tourism, a big earner before the war, is only just beginning to pick up again.
However Tudjman's popularity among ordinary citizens seems to have stayed intact despite their poverty.

After leading Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991 and steering it through the 1991-1995 war against the Serbs, he is highly praised for being a strong leader and idolised by many as "the father of the nation".
His share of the vote was thought to have been helped by strong criticism from the United States over Croatia's treatment of Serbs, which many Croats view as unjustified.
He is unlikely to enjoy any respite from Western pressure and will have to make difficult choices if Croatia is to fulfill its dream of becoming fully integrated with the West.

As well as having to meet their demands over treatment of minority Serbs and the state's stranglehold on the media, Tudjman has to ensure that the effects of economic growth, now beginning to sprout in Croatia, reach the entire population.
Tomac criticised Tudjman's ruling Croatian Democratic Union party and said if elected he would "prevent a rich elite from owning the whole country".
More than 100 delegates of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) monitored the poll. They are due to report later on Monday about the fairness of the ballot.
